## Simple explanation

A queue is like a line: the first item added is usually the first one
removed. This first-in, first-out behavior is useful when work should be
handled in arrival order.

## Technical explanation

A queue supports insertion at one end (enqueue) and removal at the other
(dequeue). Implementations may use a circular buffer, linked list, or
concurrent message service. Typical queue operations can be $O(1)$, though
the exact guarantees depend on the implementation.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Queues buffer requests between producers and consumers, help manage
asynchronous work, and can smooth uneven traffic. In model serving, queue
policy also affects latency, throughput, fairness, and cancellation.

## How it works

New work is appended, then a worker removes the oldest eligible item.
Real-world queues may include capacity limits, priorities, retries, or
multiple consumers. Systems must decide what happens when the queue is full
or a worker fails.

## Practical example

An inference service can enqueue incoming prediction requests for a worker
pool. The service may batch compatible requests, but should also enforce a
maximum wait time so requests do not sit indefinitely.

## Common misconceptions

- A queue is not necessarily durable; an in-memory queue can lose work when
  its process stops.
- FIFO ordering may not hold when priorities, retries, or multiple workers
  are involved.
